newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government unmoved on farmers' road blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greek government unmoved on farmers' road blockade.

text.p: The Greek government maintained a wait-and-see policy on a two-week farmers' protest that has paralysed transport across the country as Prime Minister Costas flew out on Wednesday to a European Union summit in Dublin.
Government spokesman Dimitris Reppas had no answers when asked how or when the government would free national highways blocked by farmers' tractors, but ruled out police intervention.
Damage from the blockade has grown. Transport Minister Haris Kastanidis said the cost to the transport sector alone was more than $90 million and rising.
State bus companies said they were suspending employees as there was no money to pay salaries. Bus services to rural areas have been virtually halted.
The Association of Northern Greek Exporters put damages for some 2,000 export firms at $400 million and said exports in December had plunged by 42 percent.
Agriculture ministry officials told Reuters that at this point the government had no option but to wait and hope that the farmers would tire and pull back their tractors.
"At some blockades the tractors are less than five. With such numbers...the country can't be held hostage. This way of protesting has no logic," Reppas told a routine news briefing.
Simitis repeated on Tuesday that Greece could not afford to satisfy the farmers' demands for cheaper fuel, equipment and higher prices.
"Demands for billions cannot be satisfied. To do so would be a step backwards," he said on Tuesday.
Simitis, who has taken a low-key approach since the protest began, left on Wednesday to attend Dublin's European Union summit. Officials said nothing could be done until his return on Sunday.

The farmers have thrown up nearly 100 road blocks with a fleet of 10,000 tractors. They said after an emergency meeting in the central farming town of Larissa that Simitis's statement was a provocation and declared they would stay put.
"We got no answer to any of our demands," said farmers' representative Thanassis Nasikas. "After the prime minister's statement we will have more tractors blocking roads."
The farmers have shown no hint of compromise, setting up sprawling tent cities on the nation's highways and blocking the borders with Turkey and Bulgaria.
The blockades have trapped foreign lorries from Europe, the Balkans and the Middle East for days, deprived of water, food and proper sanitation.
